speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what proportion of the Singapore population does the Ministry estimate has been infected with COVID-19, including unreported cases; and (b) whether Singapore has attained herd immunity with such an infection level.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: asked the Minister for Health whether an update can be provided on the study by the Health Sciences Authority and the Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination on the safety and effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines formulated for young children aged under five years old.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the Ministry plans to allow all adults below 50 years old to take their COVID-19 vaccination second booster under the National Vaccination Programme (NVP) and, if so, when is this expected; and (b) will all adults below 50 years old who wish to take their second booster due to travel requirements or concerns arising from travel plans be allowed to do so under the NVP.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Health whether the recent deaths of two young children from COVID-19 on 27 June and 17 July 2022 raised any cause for concern regarding the susceptibility of young children to the recent COVID-19 strains, bearing in mind the relatively higher number of daily reported COVID-19 cases in recent weeks and the infectiousness of the recent strains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Health whether he can provide an update on the progress of the Ministry's evaluation of (i) COVID-19 vaccines for children under five years old and (ii) other types of COVID-19 vaccines that can be administered to children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will touch on the COVID-19 situation, healthcare capacity and vaccination programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Thereafter, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will address PQs for our treatment and vaccination plans for children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if the Members who filed tomorrow's questions are satisfied with the answer, they may wish to withdraw their questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: My Deputy Speaker, we are still in the middle of an infection wave driven by the Omicron variant BA.5.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should see the wave subsiding further this week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not tighten any social restrictions during the current wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Everyone went about our lives normally: going to work, visiting families, going out with friends, travelling in and out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, life is not as normal in our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Without additional social restrictions, our healthcare system is bearing the brunt of the current wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Polyclinics and our general practitioner clinics also saw higher patient volumes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To answer Ms Joan Pereira, we are indeed promoting the use of telemedicine for mild COVID-19 cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is now a lot more accepted by patients than before.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But even so, we need to be realistic that in a big infection wave, the healthcare system will come under stress, notwithstanding the common usage of telemedicine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Waiting times at private clinics, polyclinics and hospitals will inevitably go up and I seek the patience and understanding of all our residents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In such a situation, the key is to ensure that hospitals are not overwhelmed and that those who need urgent care can be attended to promptly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By and large, we have been able to achieve that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a dynamic plan and fortunately, in the course of this infection wave, we did not have to activate all of those beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the same question, Mr Louis Chua asked about foreign patient arrivals for the last five years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think that this is a non-COVID-19 related question, we will answer it separately and Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will touch on that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, we eased the workload of hospitals by transferring lower-risk patients to COVID-19 Treatment Facilities and discharging long-term stayers back to community care facilities, like nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many of these facilities and services are run by private or social sector providers and we are deeply appreciative of them for doing this work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Compared to the last Omicron wave, the transfer processes are now a lot smoother and patients and their families have also become a lot more understanding when hospitals say that your loved one needs to be transferred.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is not ideal, because it builds up the backlog of work which have to be attended to eventually.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, the 5% cut today is far less than the 15% cut that we had to implement during the first Omicron wave in the beginning of this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hospitals restricted but did not suspend visits to patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We also did not suspend the leave of healthcare workers, so they can still take breaks, including flying to their home countries to see their loved ones and their family members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is extremely important in maintaining the morale of our healthcare workforce.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if hospital-acquired COVID-19 infections is contributing to a bed crunch.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Absenteeism in hospitals due to the current COVID-19 wave has been lower this time round, at about 2%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As far as we can determine, while there had been some transmission within hospitals, overall, hospital-acquired COVID-19 infection has been low and very likely, lower than community-acquired infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is because of good infection control measures in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to recognise that bed crunches are mainly caused by high case numbers because of an infection wave and how those case numbers translate into severe illnesses that need hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are only two ways to minimise this: one is social restrictions, two is to ensure good coverage of vaccination amongst the population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All of us do not want to bring back social restrictions as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The rule of five, the rule of two – we try to avoid that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, therefore, we need to rely on vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In that regard, like many Singaporeans, I am very proud that Singapore has achieved what many countries want to achieve, which is that most people have gotten up-to-date vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The resilience has been further strengthened as many people recovered safely from COVID-19 infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng asked what percentage of our population has been infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On record, we have about 1.7 million reported cases, which is about 30% of our population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH also systematically monitors blood samples from routine polyclinic cases and other healthy volunteers for signs of previous infection.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Notwithstanding that, this does not confer us "herd immunity".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is what enables our healthcare system to weather through an infection wave, even with high case numbers, because the translation of case numbers into severe illnesses is very low.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: During this wave, 1.9% ended up in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The actual percentages are likely to be lower because not all cases are reported.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Notwithstanding our strong resilience due to good vaccination coverage, MOH still has some concerns and we can never be complacent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First concern, coverage of the vulnerable, especially our seniors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To get good vaccine protection against severe illness from the Omicron variants, we need three doses of mRNA shots.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Another 40,000 seniors have not completed two doses yet.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All of them are vulnerable to severe illness, if infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to try to reach out to them through our Mobile Vaccination Teams, through our home vaccination teams.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second concern – MOH knows that vaccine protection against severe illness will not last forever.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, Mr Shawn Huang has, therefore, filed a very pertinent question on when this will start to wane.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the top left-hand corner, the line shows "Vaccination Effectiveness Against Severe Illness"; at the top left-hand corner is for the age group above 80; top right hand, 70 to 79; bottom, 60 to 69.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And Members can see that the graphs are not dipping; in fact, they are staying at a high level.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members will notice that at the top left-hand corner is the chart for those aged above 80.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, it has not dipped, but in general, the protection level is lower than younger cohorts, which is why we recommend that they take a fourth shot, or the second booster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for those aged 50 to 79, although the protection levels continue to be strong, this is also the age when chronic illnesses start to set in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, they have been offered the second booster if they want to take it, either because they are travelling, or they are worried about their health because of underlying chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our experts are actively studying the benefits of a fourth shot, or a second booster, for the age group of 60 to 79, in further reducing the likelihood of severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will announce their recommendations shortly, once they are ready.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the younger individuals below 60 years old, they have the protection of both the third shot, as well as age.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Currently, they do not require a second booster if they are healthy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH will continue to study the emerging data, including the benefits of newer vaccine formulations, weigh against the risk of new variants and update our recommendations, as and when necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked about the incidence of reinfections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It does occur in Singapore, but by and large, reinfection rate during the current wave has been low in Singapore and we recorded reinfection rates that are lower than many countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is likely because we have very good vaccination coverage and that we just went through a fairly large BA.2 infection wave, just at the beginning of this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH has been watching the reinfection numbers very closely, because it will inform us of the likely timing of future waves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our observation is that for those who were infected over the last three months, the chance of getting another infection is very rare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those infected four to seven months ago, the probability of getting infected again is about 3% that of an uninfected or naïve person.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you have been infected with the Delta variant last year, the probability of getting infected again is about 20% that of an uninfected person, or COVID-19-naive person.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Of course, this picture will change as time goes by and the protective effect of prior infections wanes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, having been infected by COVID-19 before, should not be a reason to let your guard down.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the meantime, reinfections are taking place, albeit not as frequently in Singapore, compared to other countries, but they are likely to increase as protection of prior infections wanes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should, therefore, start to include reinfection numbers in our daily reported case counts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the past, we report the number of patients who had been infected every day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, a patient who has been infected twice, we count him only once and there are very few of them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will be a more accurate reflection of the pandemic situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about COVID-19 therapeutics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All polyclinics and more than 130 participating PHPCs can prescribe oral antivirals to clinically eligible patients in the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To date, more than 3,200 patients have been prescribed such therapeutics across different healthcare settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a small percentage of all infections, reflective of the fact that the vast majority of infected cases are of low risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the Flu Subsidy Scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As we progress towards living with COVID-19, Singaporeans have become familiar with exercising social responsibility through self-testing by following Protocol 1-2-3.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By keeping ourselves healthy, getting up-to-date vaccinations and with employers and education institutions not always insisting to see medical certificates, most COVID-19 patients can recover uneventfully by resting at home and seeking care only when needed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our policies will, therefore, need to evolve with the state of our preparedness.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For safe management measures, we refrain from imposing additional restrictions even as we ride through a wave now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, healthcare financing policies would also need to start evolving and progressively scale back from subsidy policies that were enacted under exceptional pandemic circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want to reassure Members of the House that for residents who see their primary care doctors, they will continue to receive institutionalised, pre-COVID-19 subsidies, such as CHAS, polyclinic subsidies, health screening subsidies and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: PHPCs and polyclinics will also continue to provide Government-funded swabs to eligible symptomatic individuals at no charge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have deliberately used the term "up-to-date vaccinations", rather than a second, third or fourth booster shot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is because, at some point, just like flu vaccinations, we have to stop counting the number of boosters we have taken.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is something MOH will try to determine in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As of now, there is no change to MOH’s guidance and recommendations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to be alert to the threat of a new variant that is more infectious, leads to more severe illnesses or evades the protection of current vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We hope it will not happen, but many countries in the northern hemisphere are worried about that and what might come up in the coming winter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are riding through this current BA.5 infection wave without imposing further social restrictions or imposing border measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In our hospitals, we imposed fewer restrictions and hospitals are, generally, able to cope better than the last wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means that the Singapore society has taken another major step forward in living with COVID-19 as an endemic disease and I think this is a big National Day present for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I was saddened by the recent deaths of two young children from COVID-19 and offer my deepest condolences to their families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Based on local and international data, the BA.4 and BA.5 Omicron subvariants have not been observed to affect children more severely than past variants and severe COVID-19 infection continues to be rare in children, especially amongst those who are vaccinated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At present, the Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty COVID-19 vaccine remains the only vaccine authorised for use in children aged five to 17 in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Children who are not medically eligible for the Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty COVID-19 vaccine may receive the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccine under a dedicated public health programme, while Moderna’s vaccine for this age group remains under evaluation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Children under the age of five are, currently, the last group not yet protected by vaccination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Health Sciences Authority (HSA) is currently reviewing the data submitted by Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna on their COVID-19 vaccines for this age group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will provide an update when an assessment of the quality, effectiveness and safety of the vaccines has been completed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Members asked what could be done to detect, diagnose and treat COVID-19 in children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Currently, children under the age of five remain more vulnerable to COVID-19 infection and have higher rates of severe outcomes, as compared to older children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: However, the overall incidence of severe outcomes from COVID-19 infection remains much lower amongst children, compared to adults and the elderly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Children needing medical attention should be seen by a general practitioner (GP) or polyclinic if unwell and the clinical team, the doctors there, will test children with acute respiratory infection (ARI) symptoms using an Antigen Rapid Test (ART) by default or a Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test, if indicated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Children under three months of age are admitted to hospital by default, whereas older children are treated under the Home Recovery Programme (HRP) and reviewed by doctors via telemedicine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our hospitals continue to prioritise care for children with urgent medical conditions and those who require further observation and treatment will be admitted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH regularly reviews and updates the screening and review criteria with inputs from a panel of specialists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Oral antivirals are licensed for use under HSA’s Pandemic Special Access Route for patients aged 18 and above only.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For children aged between 12 and 18, local and overseas treatment guidelines indicate that Paxlovid may be considered on a case-to-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to review the evidence for the use of oral antivirals for children under 18 years of age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to monitor the incidence of severe illness and deaths due to COVID-19 closely and adjust our processes to protect our healthcare system and patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We ask everyone to take the necessary precautions and remain socially responsible by self-testing if unwell, getting vaccinated and boosted, and avoiding social interactions if you have a fever or respiratory symptoms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Lastly, Sir, to address Mr Louis Chua's question on foreign patients, the number of foreign patients who come to Singapore to specifically seek inpatient treatment or day surgery at our hospitals has, historically, been small.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These numbers have since fallen by 80%, compared to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In 2021, there were just 6,000 episodes, comprising less than 1% of total cases seen in hospitals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A recent study from Portugal suggested that the current lead dominant Omicron BA.5 subvariant is linked with higher odds of causing reinfection, regardless of the vaccination status.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is the Ministry considering conducting similar studies and would such findings affect our country's vaccination and treatment strategies?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have reported just now, MOH, likewise, is monitoring empirically the rate of reinfections in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By and large, we have noticed that our rate of reinfection is lower than many other countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are at a stage where every country's experience is different because they experienced different waves with different dominant strains and different vaccination and booster rates and also different age profiles, old and young.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, when you take all that into account, every country's experience is now unique.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, Portugal has gone through a wave with many hospitalisations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Australia is undergoing a BA.5 wave with many hospitalisations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to monitor the reinfection rate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have mentioned, what is important is whether reinfections or infections translate into hospitalisations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, what is important is vaccination effectiveness against severe illness.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have mentioned and as I have shown in the chart earlier, after 10 months, the protective effect is still strong but we will monitor closely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have two supplementary questions which are related to the PQ which the Minister probably did not get the chance to answer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first is whether the Flu Subsidy Scheme has encouraged more eligible residents to seek medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the reasons I asked the PQ for tomorrow is that some residents have come to me on the scheme because they have found it to be useful, especially in the current context of rising costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second supplementary question is with regard to the deactivation of the scheme, whether it will hamper early detection of efforts in terms of data collection for COVID-19 by MOH as well, going forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Does the Flu Subsidy Scheme increase the number of people seeking medical treatment?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I believe that is a reasonable effect that we should expect of any subsidy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think in the community, we have seen and we have probably met residents who say, "Since there is the Flu Subsidy Scheme and it costs $10, no harm.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Just go to the GP," and when they are very well, young and probably can recover uneventfully at home, drinking more water, rest, taking ART.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think, when we have a subsidy scheme like that, on the one hand, more people may come forward; on the other hand, you can also overcrowd the GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is what we are trying to do for one of our smaller schemes, which is Flu Subsidy Scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that is an even larger amount that we continue to support.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Will this therefore reduce the detection rate of COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think a lot depends on self-testing, much more than testing at the GPs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You can now use telemedicine, as Ms Joan Pereira said.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Using telemedicine, test in front of a camera on Zoom and the doctor can record it in the system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, by and large, people know how to use the system and we continue to be able to monitor our epi curve with the reports from people, very promptly and quite accurately.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just three supplementary questions for the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could he give us a sense of that data for the non-mRNA vaccines, the traditional vaccines?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second supplementary question is: would MOH consider sending mobile vaccination teams to individual homes to vaccinate them even if they are not seniors, if there are strong mitigating factors?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, if the individual is diagnosed with a mental health condition that makes it hard for them to leave their home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The third supplementary question is: would the Ministry consider tweaking its systems and processes to encourage people who go for the COVID-19 vaccines to also get the regular flu vaccine at the same time if, indeed, that is scientifically feasible?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Novavax has shown to be efficacious in preventing severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the data has shown that these are slightly less efficacious; not just us, but Chile, Malaysia and other countries have also published similar data and admit similar observations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, they do have a protective effect.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having those vaccinations is better than not having vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you come across any residents that need them, you can always raise with MOH and we will assess and try to be as helpful as we can.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But unlike many other countries where there are four seasons and there is a winter and a flu season, they find it useful to administer flu vaccines and COVID-19 vaccines concurrently, which is what Australia is doing currently.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And towards the fall, many Northern Hemisphere countries intend to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is harder for us to combine two vaccinations at the same time because of the lack of a flu season.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if someone wants both together, we should think of a way to administer both.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, Minister mentioned that the current 60% infection does not accord us "herd immunity".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I would just like to ask at what level would it be considered that we have "herd immunity"?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My second supplementary question relates to the seniors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am concerned that there are 80,000 of our seniors who either have not gotten their second vaccination or have not had the booster jab.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Eighty thousand seniors is a lot of people.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I know we are still trying to reach out to them through our mobile vaccination teams.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think that will take too long; we have been trying that for quite a while.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think to cover the entire 80,000 will take a long, long time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, my question is: what other solutions are there beyond the current mobile vaccination teams?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is no longer a function or percentage coverage of vaccinations or infections but it is the fact that it is a fast mutating virus and it will escape prior infection protection as well as vaccine protection.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, therefore, do not aim for "herd immunity" where we think the virus will disappear but instead live with the virus and protect ourselves against severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are very, very high by international standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I suspect, especially the 40,000 seniors who have not even taken two shots, they must have deep personal reasons not to do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the other 40,000, they have taken two shots but somehow have not taken the booster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For them, I am a bit more sanguine because they have taken two before; I think we can persuade them to take a third.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But those who have not taken, we have met them and we have tried to persuade them; it is difficult.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The better way now is for us to be considerate that there are such vulnerable seniors amongst us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we must always exercise our social responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we do not feel well when we are meeting one of these seniors, avoid meeting them or test yourself before you meet them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In other words, the rest of us who have been vaccinated or have been infected, we have to protect those who are not protected and are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I just want to seek clarification from the Minister regarding my Question No 13, part (b).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am not sure I heard the answer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For Singaporeans under 50, if they wish to take the second booster because of travel requirements or because of concerns arising out of travel, will they be allowed to do so under the National Vaccination Programme?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are below 50, you have taken three shots already and you are healthy, our rules do not provide for them and they would not be offered.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if they have underlying conditions and they suspect they are sick, they can let us know and we will offer it to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The reason is, as I mentioned earlier, protection against severe illness is what is important and it continues to stay very high, especially if you are young.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And towards year end, we do not know what is coming our way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the Northern Hemisphere, many countries are worried about new variants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, therefore, sometimes, it is also worthwhile to keep our powder dry, especially for the younger group.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We will take the last two questions on this topic.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and then Mr Louis Chua.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have one clarification for the Minister on whether his response on hospital-acquired infections include our community hospitals and nursing homes, because many of the patients there are seniors and vulnerable patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And thankfully, we have been able to keep our nursing homes safe.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to try hard to protect our nursing homes and community hospitals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I just have one supplementary question for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On 9 May, in a report in The Straits Times, one of the private hospital groups shared that it has stood down its ringfenced general ward capacity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note from the Minister's response that about 1,000 hospital beds are being set aside for COVID-19 purposes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I just wanted to understand – the healthcare system today across both the public and private hospitals, what is the current level of bed utilisation as a whole?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And if the need arises, where would these additional 1,000 beds come from and how quickly can they be activated?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we include private hospital beds that we can acquire, that is another couple hundred more – I cannot remember the number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, hospitals are busy, not because of COVID-19 patients, but a lot of business-as-usual patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this is after taking into account, setting aside some beds for COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned, it is a dynamic plan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we see a curve going down, numbers going down, we may release more beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we see the epi curve going up, we may take out more beds and inch towards the 1,000-bed scenario.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But what is important, what I mentioned, is that for this wave, we managed to ride through it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We managed to go through it better prepared and better response than the last wave.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Because the presentation of the Petition took six minutes, I have been informed that Question Time will be extended to 3.06 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, we can carry on with the PQs.
